What is an ordinary, nonindexed SQL Server view?
column2:
A virtual table defined by a query.
Its result set is not stored separately from the underlying data.
Review source

column1: How does a view simplify a frequently reused join?
column2:
It hides the join behind a reusable table-like interface.
Applications query the view instead of repeating the join logic.
Review source

column1: Why put a shared calculation, such as order categorization, in a view?
column2:
To define the calculation once for all callers.
Each query through the view uses the same calculation logic.
Review source

column1: Which part of a view definition limits the rows that it exposes?
column2:
Its WHERE clause.
For example, WHERE IsActive = 1 exposes only active customers.
Review source

column1: Which part of a view definition controls the columns that it exposes?
column2:
Its SELECT list.
Omit sensitive columns that the view's callers do not need.
Review source

column1: What permission pattern supports restricted data access through a view?
column2:
Grant SELECT on the view and restrict direct access to its base tables.
A view does not remove existing permissions to read the underlying tables.
Review source

column1: Why list view columns explicitly instead of using SELECT *?
column2:
To keep the exposed columns deliberate and stable.
Underlying schema changes can otherwise cause unexpected results from a non-schema-bound view.
Review source

column1: Why keep a view focused on one purpose?
column2:
To make its query logic easier to understand and optimize.
Separate use cases can use separate views instead of one overloaded definition.
Review source

column1: What does WITH CHECK OPTION enforce on an otherwise updatable view?
column2:
Inserted or updated rows must remain visible through the view.
The resulting row must satisfy the view's filter.
Review source

column1: Which modifications bypass a view's WITH CHECK OPTION?
column2:
Modifications made directly to its base tables.
The option applies only to changes made through the view.
Review source

column1: Without an INSTEAD OF trigger, how many base tables can one UPDATE through a view modify?
column2:
One base table for an ordinary view, including a joined view.
Updatable UNION ALL partitioned views are a special exception with additional restrictions.
Review source

column1: Without an INSTEAD OF trigger, why cannot a view's CASE-derived column be assigned a value directly?
column2:
It does not directly reference an updatable base-table column.
SQL Server cannot map the assigned value back to a base-table column.
Review source

column1: Which type of SQL Server view physically stores its result set?
column2:
An indexed view, also called a materialized view.
Azure SQL and Fabric SQL database also support indexed views. Fabric Warehouse does not support materialized views.
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column1: What maintains an indexed view's stored results when its base-table data changes?
column2:
SQL Server updates the indexed view as part of the data modification.
The stored results are maintained, not frozen at creation time.
Review source

column1: Why does an ordinary view not automatically make a query faster?
column2:
Its underlying query still requires execution.
A view encapsulates query logic rather than guaranteeing a cached result.
Review source

column1: Which SQL object provides reusable, parameterized query logic that returns a table?
column2:
A table-valued function.
An ordinary view does not declare input parameters.
Review source

column1: Which SQL object is generally better than a view for complex data-modification logic?
column2:
A stored procedure.
Views primarily present reusable query results rather than define modification workflows.
Review source

column1: How do you query an existing SQL Server view?
column2:
Reference its name in a SELECT statement's FROM clause.
You can add a WHERE clause to filter the view's results further.
Review source
